newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir hostages' relatives appeal for their release.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir hostages' relatives appeal for their release.

text.p: The families of two Britons taken hostage by guerrillas in Kashmir nearly two years ago appealed to the public on Monday for news, good or bad, about their kidnapped relatives.
"For over 21 months, we have been kept in an agonising situation, not knowing the truth. We want the truth, be it good or bad," Bob Wells, father of hostage Paul Wells, told a news conference.
"Any information, old or new, will help ease our pain," he said. "We hope they are alive, but nobody has any certain information. We only wish for our loved ones to be returned to us."

Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells, and four other Western tourists were abducted by the shadowy Al-Faran militant group in July 1995. An American escaped and a Norwegian, Hans Christian Ostroe, was found beheaded in August 1995.
Authorities have detected no trace of Mangan, Wells, American Donald Hutchings or German Dirk Hasert for months.
Bob Wells was accompanied by Paul's girlfriend Catherine Moseley, Mangan's wife Julie and a cousin of hers who is heading a campaign in Britain to free the hostages.

The four Britons plan to spend the next three weeks meeting officials in India, travelling through Kashmir and on to Pakistan to appeal to the people for news about their loved ones, Mangan said. India controls two-thirds of Kashmir and Pakistan the rest.
She said they would circulate leaflets in Urdu, with a photograph of the hostages on it, appealing for help.
"We want to speak to anybody who can help us," Mangan said. "People tell us what they think we want to hear, but if they're dead, God forbid, we just want to hear the truth."
British diplomats said it had been several months since the hostages were last spotted, raising doubts about whether they were still alive.
Mangan, 35, said she hoped to convey her appeal to shepherds in Jammu, the winter capital of the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir, who would be returning to mountains in summer.
"They are really the key people to spread the message. Hopefully our message will get to our men," she said.
Moseley, 27, said she was hoping former Al-Faran members or relatives of the rebels would respond to their appeal.
"Someone there has to have a conscience," she told Reuters. "If they are dead, we want to know. It would make it a lot less difficult. We just cannot go on like this."
